title: What are the stages of a CI/CD pipeline (source → build → test → package → scan → deploy → verify), and what is the difference between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment?
shortTitle: CI/CD Pipeline Stages and the Difference Between Continuous Integration, Delivery and Deployment

s1_definition.profdef: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that takes a code change from a developer's commit all the way to a running environment. The typical stages are source (fetch the commit), build (compile and assemble artifacts), test (run unit and integration tests), package (produce a deployable artifact such as a JAR or container image), scan (static analysis and vulnerability scanning), deploy (push to an environment), and verify (smoke tests and health checks). Continuous Integration is the practice of merging and automatically building and testing every change frequently. Continuous Delivery extends CI so that every passing build is automatically prepared and ready for release, but the final push to production is a manual approval. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and releases every passing build to production automatically with no human gate.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's cheque clearing line. A cheque (a code change) arrives at the counter (source). It is first read and stamped (build), then verified against the signature and balance (test), then put into a sealed clearing envelope (package), then checked for forgery and fraud (scan), then sent to the destination branch (deploy), and finally the destination branch confirms it landed correctly (verify). Continuous Integration is Rajesh and Priya both dropping their cheques into the same clearing line many times a day and the machine immediately checking each one. Continuous Delivery means every verified cheque is packed and sitting ready at the vault door, but a manager must press the button to release it. Continuous Deployment means the machine releases it automatically with no manager needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: CI proves the code is good, Continuous Delivery keeps it release-ready behind a button, and Continuous Deployment presses that button automatically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that takes a code change from a developer's commit all the way to a running environment. The typical stages are source (fetch the commit), build (compile and assemble artifacts), test (run unit and integration tests), package (produce a deployable artifact such as a JAR or container image), scan (static analysis and vulnerability scanning), deploy (push to an environment), and verify (smoke tests and health checks). Continuous Integration is the practice of merging and automatically building and testing every change frequently. Continuous Delivery extends CI so that every passing build is automatically prepared and ready for release, but the final push to production is a manual approval. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and releases every passing build to production automatically with no human gate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's cheque clearing line. A cheque (a code change) arrives at the counter (source). It is first read and stamped (build), then verified against the signature and balance (test), then put into a sealed clearing envelope (package), then checked for forgery and fraud (scan), then sent to the destination branch (deploy), and finally the destination branch confirms it landed correctly (verify). Continuous Integration is Rajesh and Priya both dropping their cheques into the same clearing line many times a day and the machine immediately checking each one. Continuous Delivery means every verified cheque is packed and sitting ready at the vault door, but a manager must press the button to release it. Continuous Deployment means the machine releases it automatically with no manager needed.

**One line to remember:** CI proves the code is good, Continuous Delivery keeps it release-ready behind a button, and Continuous Deployment presses that button automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
The source stage is where the pipeline begins. A trigger such as a Git push or a merged pull request causes the CI server to check out the exact commit. For example, a Jenkins pipeline step `checkout scm` or a GitHub Actions step `uses: actions/checkout@v4` pulls the banking service source at a known SHA so every later stage works on identical code.

The build stage compiles the source and assembles the primary artifact. For a Spring Boot banking service this is usually `mvn clean package -DskipTests` which produces a runnable JAR. Separating build from test lets you fail fast on compilation errors before spending time running tests.

The test stage runs automated tests. Unit tests run first because they are fast, for example `mvn test` running a `TransferServiceTest` that checks a debit and credit leave balances correct. Integration tests run next, often against a throwaway database spun up with Testcontainers, so a `TransferControllerIT` can verify the real HTTP endpoint and the real SQL. A failing test here stops the pipeline so broken code never reaches an environment.

The package stage turns the tested code into a deployable unit. In a container world this is building an image, for example `docker build -t registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2 .` and tagging it with the build number so the exact artifact is traceable.

The scan stage enforces quality and security. Static analysis with SonarQube checks code smells and coverage and can fail the build if a quality gate is breached. Vulnerability scanning with Trivy checks the image layers and dependencies, for example `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2`, which fails the pipeline if a critical CVE is present in a library the banking service pulls in.

The deploy stage pushes the artifact to an environment. This might be `kubectl set image deployment/transfer-service transfer-service=registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2` for a Kubernetes rollout, or a Helm upgrade. In a mature setup deployment is split per environment: dev first, then QA, then production.

The verify stage confirms the deployment is actually healthy. A smoke test calls the live health endpoint, for example `curl -f https://transfer.bank.local/actuator/health`, and a few business smoke checks confirm a test transfer succeeds. If verify fails, the pipeline rolls back.

The three terms differ by how far automation reaches. Continuous Integration stops at a green build and test. Continuous Delivery automates everything up to a production-ready artifact but keeps a manual approval before production, which is common in banking because a human must sign off before touching the live ledger. Continuous Deployment removes even that gate, so every green build reaches customers automatically. A senior nuance is that regulated banking systems almost always use Continuous Delivery to production with an approval, while using full Continuous Deployment freely for lower environments like dev and QA.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh commits a change to the transfer service that accidentally breaks the fee calculation. In the old days nobody noticed until a tester manually ran the app days later, by which time three more changes had piled on top and it was impossible to tell which commit broke it. This is exactly the problem Continuous Integration solves. Every commit is built and tested automatically within minutes, so the moment Rajesh's bad fee logic lands, the pipeline fails and points straight at his commit.

Problem 2 — Even when the code is good, the team used to deploy by hand, copying JARs onto servers at midnight. One engineer deployed the wrong version to production and a day of transfers used stale fee tables. This is exactly the problem a packaging and deploy pipeline solves. The pipeline builds one immutable artifact, tags it with the commit, and that exact artifact is what gets promoted through dev, QA, and production, so there is never a mismatch.

Problem 3 — A security audit found that a vulnerable logging library had been running in production for months. Nobody scanned artifacts before release. This is exactly the problem the scan stage solves. Every image is scanned for known vulnerabilities and the build fails if a critical issue is present, so vulnerable code is blocked before it ever reaches the banking environment.

To make this concrete without a real Jenkins server, we will write a small Java program that simulates a CI/CD pipeline. We will model each stage as a class implementing a common `PipelineStage` interface. We will have a `SourceStage`, `BuildStage`, `TestStage`, `PackageStage`, `ScanStage`, `DeployStage`, and `VerifyStage`. A `Pipeline` orchestrator runs them in order, stops on the first failure, and prints a clear report. We will run it once for a healthy commit that passes all stages and once for a commit with a failing test so you can see the pipeline stop early. This mirrors the real behaviour where a red stage halts promotion to the next environment.

```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the pipeline simulation
java -cp target/classes com.bank.cicd.PipelineDemo

# In a real pipeline you would instead run the stages directly:
mvn clean package
docker build -t registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2 .
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a Git commit identified by a SHA. We run two: the healthy commit `a1b2c3-healthy` and the broken commit `x9y8z7-bad-test`.

Step 1: For the healthy commit, the SourceStage receives the SHA, confirms it is non-blank, and returns success with the message that it checked out the commit. The data at this point is just the identifier of the change.

Step 2: The BuildStage runs and reports that it compiled the transfer service and produced the JAR. Nothing about the commit identifier changes; we are now holding a built artifact conceptually.

Step 3: The TestStage inspects the commit identifier. Because it does not contain the marker `bad-test`, it returns success with 42 tests passing and 86% coverage. The gate stays green.

Step 4: The PackageStage builds an image tag by appending the SHA to the registry path, producing `registry.bank.local/transfer-service:a1b2c3-healthy`. The artifact is now immutable and traceable to the commit.

Step 5: The ScanStage checks for the marker `cve`, does not find it, and returns success with the quality gate passed and Trivy clean.

Step 6: The DeployStage reports the image rolled out to dev. Step 7: the VerifyStage reports the health check up and a smoke transfer from SAV2001 to CUR3001 succeeded. The pipeline prints overall success and promotes the artifact.

Step 8: For the broken commit, stages one and two pass, but at the TestStage the identifier contains `bad-test`, so it returns failure. The orchestrator logs the failure and immediately halts, so the package, scan, deploy, and verify stages never run and nothing broken reaches an environment.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence that carries a code change from commit to a running environment through well-defined stages: source checks out the exact commit, build compiles and assembles the artifact, test runs unit and integration tests, package produces an immutable deployable such as a container image tagged with the commit, scan runs static analysis and vulnerability checks with quality gates, deploy pushes to an environment, and verify confirms health with smoke tests. The key design principle is fail fast and promote only what is proven, so a red stage immediately halts promotion and nothing broken moves forward.

The three terms are often confused, so I keep them precise. Continuous Integration is the discipline of merging every change frequently and automatically building and testing it, which catches integration problems within minutes rather than days. Continuous Delivery extends that so every passing build is automatically prepared as a release-ready artifact, but the final push to production stays behind a manual approval. Continuous Deployment removes even that gate and releases every green build straight to production automatically.

In banking the distinction matters a lot. At the National Bank of India we ran full Continuous Deployment in the dev and QA environments because speed there is pure upside, but production used Continuous Delivery with a human approval gate, because a regulator and an auditor expect a named person to sign off before the live ledger changes. That approval was not a bottleneck because everything before it was automated and the artifact was already proven.

On the project I built a pipeline for the transfer service where every commit was built, tested against a Testcontainers Postgres, scanned with SonarQube for a coverage and quality gate, and scanned with Trivy for critical CVEs, and only then packaged into an image tagged with the commit SHA. That tagged image was the single artifact promoted through every environment, which eliminated the classic problem of deploying the wrong version. The senior point I always add is that the artifact must be immutable and traceable to a commit, and that verify is not optional — a deploy that is not confirmed healthy is treated as a failure and rolled back automatically.

---

keyPoints: CI: automated build + test on every commit
Pipeline stages: build -> test -> security scan -> deploy
